text: Ahithophel told Absalom to let him pick twelve thousand men and set out after David that very night.
He would catch David while he was tired and discouraged and throw him into a panic, so that everyone with him would scatter, and he would strike down the king alone.
Then he would bring the rest of the people back to Absalom peacefully, the way a bride comes home to her husband, since it was only one man's life being sought, leaving everyone else unharmed.
The plan sounded good to Absalom and to all of Israel's elders.
Even so, Absalom said to call Hushai the Archite too, so they could hear what he thought.
When Hushai arrived, Absalom told him what Ahithophel had proposed and asked whether they should follow it, or whether Hushai had something else to say.
Hushai replied that this time, Ahithophel's advice was not good.

He reminded Absalom that his father and his men were seasoned fighters, as dangerous right now as a wild bear robbed of her cubs, and that David, an experienced soldier, would never simply camp out in the open with his troops.
He said David was probably already hidden in a cave or somewhere similar, and if David's men struck first, word would spread that Absalom's side had suffered a defeat.
Then, Hushai warned, even Absalom's bravest fighters, however lion-hearted, would lose their nerve, because everyone in Israel already knew David and his men were formidable warriors.
His own advice was to gather every tribe of Israel together, as numerous as sand on the seashore, and have Absalom personally lead them into battle himself.
That way, he said, they would find David wherever he was and overwhelm him the way dew covers the ground at dawn, leaving not a single man of his company alive.
And if David retreated into some city, all Israel would bring ropes and drag that city down into the valley until not even a stone of it remained.

Absalom and the men of Israel agreed that Hushai's advice was better than Ahithophel's — though in truth the LORD himself had arranged for Ahithophel's sound counsel to be rejected, in order to bring ruin on Absalom.
Hushai then told the priests Zadok and Abiathar exactly what Ahithophel had advised and what he himself had advised instead.
He urged them to get word to David right away not to camp overnight at the crossing points of the wilderness, but to cross the river without delay, or he and everyone with him could be wiped out.
Jonathan and Ahimaaz were staying near En-rogel, since they couldn't risk being seen going into the city, and a servant girl was supposed to bring them the message to carry on to David.
But a boy spotted them and reported it to Absalom, so the two men hurried off and reached the house of a man in Bahurim who had a well in his yard, and they climbed down into it.
The man's wife spread a cover over the well's opening and scattered grain on top of it so nothing looked out of place.

When Absalom's men reached the house and asked the woman where Ahimaaz and Jonathan were, she told them they had gone on across the stream; the men searched, found nothing, and went back to Jerusalem.
Once the searchers had left, the two climbed out of the well and hurried to tell David to cross the water immediately, since Ahithophel had advised moving against him.
So David and everyone with him got up and crossed the Jordan, and by the time morning came, not a single person was left who hadn't crossed.
When Ahithophel realized his advice had been ignored, he saddled his donkey and went home to his own town, put his affairs in order, and hanged himself; he was buried in his father's tomb.
David arrived at Mahanaim about the same time Absalom and all the men of Israel crossed the Jordan.
Absalom had put Amasa in charge of the army in Joab's place — Amasa's father was Ithra the Ishmaelite, who had married Abigail, daughter of Nahash and sister to Joab's mother Zeruiah.
Israel's forces, with Absalom, set up camp in the region of Gilead.
When David got to Mahanaim, Shobi son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites, along with Machir son of Ammiel from Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Rogelim,
brought bedding, basins, pottery, wheat, barley, flour, roasted grain, beans, and lentils,
plus honey, curds, sheep, and cheese, for David and his people to eat, since they figured the men had grown hungry, tired, and thirsty out in the wilderness.
